title: How cancer cells cheat
blurb: Dodging death, dividing endlessly, and feeding themselves, in real data.
review: Needs expert check: the interpretation of BCR knockdown as BCR-ABL1 loss, and the erythroid-gene reading.

text.simple: K562 cancer cells have two genes accidentally glued together, **BCR** and **ABL1**. The glued-together protein is always on and keeps shouting 'grow!'
text.student: In chronic myeloid leukemia, a swap between chromosomes 9 and 22 (the 'Philadelphia chromosome') fuses BCR to ABL1. The BCR-ABL1 protein is a kinase that's permanently on. [@lozzio1975] [@druker2001]
text.deep: BCR-ABL1 is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase signaling through GRB2/SOS/RAS, PI3K/AKT and STAT5, promoting proliferation and survival (e.g., via BCL-XL). [@weinberg]

steps.title: Try it: turn off the fusion

note.simple: In K562, the top changed genes are linked to making red blood cells. Without its cheat code, the leukemia cell starts acting more like a normal blood cell. In the healthy-like cell, very different genes change.
note.student: ● Measured in both. In K562, BCR knockdown (which also silences the fusion) raises genes such as **SLC25A37** and **BLVRB**, linked to red-blood-cell maturation. In RPE1 it mostly changes cytoskeleton genes. Same action, very different meaning.
note.deep: The K562 signature is consistent with erythroid differentiation reported after BCR-ABL1 inhibition in K562 (an interpretation worth expert review). Pathway-level scores are modest; the signal is concentrated in specific genes.

text.simple: What happens if we switch off BCR-ABL1?
text.student: Compare the two cells' top genes.
text.deep: Inspect the top genes rather than the pathway bars here.

note.simple: mTOR is a master growth switch. Turning it off quiets lots of pathways in **both** cells. It's important for every cell, not just cancer.
note.student: ● Measured: MTOR knockdown lowers division, energy and DNA-repair programs in both cell lines. A drug hitting mTOR would likely affect healthy cells too.
note.deep: MTOR knockdown produces broad, shared downregulation across programs in both lines, with a paradoxical rise in translation-gene mRNAs (possibly compensatory). mRNA ≠ translation rate.

text.simple: Cancer cells need lots of energy and building blocks to keep making copies of themselves.
text.student: Growth switches like **mTOR** coordinate nutrients, energy and protein-making. Cancers often keep them on. [@hanahan2011]
text.deep: mTORC1 integrates growth factor, nutrient and energy signals to drive anabolism. [@vanderheiden2009]

try.note: Two anti-death guards turned off at once. This combination is ◐ predicted by adding up the two measured single effects.

text.simple: Cancer cells put extra guards on their self-destruct button. What if we remove two guards at once?
text.student: Combining knockdowns of **BCL-XL** and **MCL1** removes two layers of protection against apoptosis. [@hanahan2011]
text.deep: Dual BCL-XL/MCL1 dependence is common; additive transcriptional models can't capture the synthetic-lethal cell death that may result (dead cells aren't sequenced).

text.simple: Big secret: if a cell dies, we can't measure it anymore! So this data shows how cells change *before* they die, not who dies.
text.student: Perturb-seq measures gene activity in cells that survive long enough to be sequenced. Strong 'killer' knockdowns may look weaker than they are. [@replogle2022]
text.deep: Survivorship bias: strongly lethal perturbations are sampled with fewer cells and in surviving states; fitness effects are better read from proliferation screens.
